scenes.visual: Dark slate background (#0F172A), reusing the exact colour map from the first film. Center-frame: the slate-blue early endosome rimmed with cyan Rab5 (#38BDF8) and soft amber lumen, carrying an emerald signaling receptor (#34D399) whose glowing tail extends into the cytosol. Centered white title (size 48): 'Still Talking, Until Sealed Inside'.

scenes.tts: In the first film, internalized receptors reached the early endosome with their tails still facing the cytosol. Can an active receptor keep signaling from there, and what finally shuts it off? Surprisingly, entering the cell does not by itself silence an active receptor.
scenes.caption: In the first film, internalized receptors reached the early endosome with their tails still facing the cytosol. Can an active receptor keep signaling from there, and what finally shuts it off? Surprisingly, entering the cell does not by itself silence an active receptor.
scenes.visual: Title fades out. Keep the same slate-blue plasma membrane at top and cyan Rab5 early endosome below (filling 60% of frame height, schematic). Follow an emerald active receptor (#34D399, ligand still bound) moving from the surface to the outer membrane of the early endosome; a pulsing green halo around its cytoplasmic tail stays bright in the cytosol. Clean question label appears at upper right: 'Still signaling?'
scenes.narration: In the first film, internalized receptors reached the early endosome with their tails still facing the cytosol. Can an active receptor keep signaling from there, and what finally shuts it off? Surprisingly, entering the cell does not by itself silence an active receptor.

scenes.tts: Inside the cell sounds isolated, yet the way the membrane faces says otherwise. On the outer endosome membrane, an active receptor's tail still touches cytosolic partner proteins. Some receptors keep sending the same signal. Others even switch partners once they leave the plasma membrane.
scenes.caption: Inside the cell sounds isolated, yet the way the membrane faces says otherwise. On the outer endosome membrane, an active receptor's tail still touches cytosolic partner proteins. Some receptors keep sending the same signal. Others even switch partners once they leave the plasma membrane.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the outer wall of the cyan Rab5 early endosome (schematic). Highlight the label 'Tail in cytosol' beside the emerald receptor's glowing cytoplasmic tail. Cytosolic partner blocks drift in from the dark navy cytosol and dock onto the exposed tail, triggering gentle outward signal ripples.
scenes.narration: Inside the cell sounds isolated, yet the way the membrane faces says otherwise. On the outer endosome membrane, an active receptor's tail still touches cytosolic partner proteins. Some receptors keep sending the same signal. Others even switch partners once they leave the plasma membrane.

scenes.tts: Toll-like receptor four shows that location switch clearly. At the plasma membrane, it binds a cytosolic adaptor called my D eighty eight. After endocytosis into an endosome, it binds a second adaptor, called triff, which switches on interferon genes.
scenes.caption: Toll-like receptor 4 shows that location switch clearly. At the plasma membrane, it binds a cytosolic adaptor called MyD88. After endocytosis into an endosome, it binds a second adaptor, called TRIF, which switches on interferon genes.
scenes.visual: Split vertical view of the same cell world (schematic): top, emerald receptor labelled 'TLR4' sits at the slate-blue plasma membrane binding a sky-blue block ('MyD88'). The same emerald TLR4 moves downward in a vesicle into the cyan Rab5 early endosome below; MyD88 releases and a bright lime-gold block ('TRIF') docks onto its exposed cytosolic tail, sending a labeled pulse 'Interferon genes' into the cytosol.
scenes.narration: Toll-like receptor 4 shows that location switch clearly. At the plasma membrane, it binds a cytosolic adaptor called MyD88. After endocytosis into an endosome, it binds a second adaptor, called TRIF, which switches on interferon genes.

scenes.tts: So how does a cell silence an endosomal receptor? A receptor leaves the recycling route when an enzyme attaches a small tag called ubiquitin. A protein complex on the endosome, called Escort, reads ubiquitin and gathers tagged receptors into one patch.
scenes.caption: So how does a cell silence an endosomal receptor? A receptor leaves the recycling route when an enzyme attaches a small tag called ubiquitin. A protein complex on the endosome, called ESCRT, reads ubiquitin and gathers tagged receptors into one patch.
scenes.visual: Return focus to the cyan Rab5 early endosome with active emerald receptors (#34D399) on its outer membrane (schematic). Bright gold-yellow beads (#FACC15, label 'Ubiquitin') attach to their cytosolic tails. Crisp rose-red clamps (#F43F5E, label 'ESCRT') assemble on the outer face, grip the gold ubiquitin tags, and slide the tagged emerald receptors together into one dense patch away from the mint-teal recycling tubules.
scenes.narration: So how does a cell silence an endosomal receptor? A receptor leaves the recycling route when an enzyme attaches a small tag called ubiquitin. A protein complex on the endosome, called ESCRT, reads ubiquitin and gathers tagged receptors into one patch.

scenes.tts: Watch which way Escort bends the membrane. Coated pits pulled membrane into the cytosol, leaving tails exposed. Escort pushes the tagged patch the opposite way, inward into the endosome fluid. It pinches off as a small vesicle inside a multivesicular endosome.
scenes.caption: Watch which way ESCRT bends the membrane. Coated pits pulled membrane into the cytosol, leaving tails exposed. ESCRT pushes the tagged patch the opposite way, inward into the endosome fluid. It pinches off as a small vesicle inside a multivesicular endosome.
scenes.visual: Rose-red ESCRT clamps (#F43F5E) push the ubiquitin-tagged patch of slate-blue membrane inward, away from the cytosol, into the amber lumen (bold directional arrow 'Inward bud', schematic). The inward bud deepens and pinches off cleanly as a free small bubble inside the endosome, carrying the emerald receptor. Label appears: 'Multivesicular endosome'.
scenes.narration: Watch which way ESCRT bends the membrane. Coated pits pulled membrane into the cytosol, leaving tails exposed. ESCRT pushes the tagged patch the opposite way, inward into the endosome fluid. It pinches off as a small vesicle inside a multivesicular endosome.

scenes.tts: Check which way the receptor tail faces now. The receptor sits sealed inside that internal vesicle before any lysosome arrives. Does its signal stop right now, or only after digestive enzymes break it down?
scenes.caption: Check which way the receptor tail faces now. The receptor sits sealed inside that internal vesicle before any lysosome arrives. Does its signal stop right now, or only after digestive enzymes break it down?
scenes.visual: Zoom tightly onto the internal vesicle floating inside the multivesicular endosome (schematic). Cytosolic partner proteins hover outside the outer endosome membrane while the emerald receptor's tail points inward inside the tiny inner bubble, separated by two membranes. High-contrast question card fades in at the bottom: 'Signal stops now, or only in the lysosome?'
scenes.narration: Check which way the receptor tail faces now. The receptor sits sealed inside that internal vesicle before any lysosome arrives. Does its signal stop right now, or only after digestive enzymes break it down?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card 'Signal stops now, or only in the lysosome?' on screen. Keep slow ambient motion: cytosolic partner blocks bounce gently off the outer endosome wall unable to cross, the tiny internal vesicle drifts slowly inside the amber lumen, and a subtle progress bar ticks across the bottom.

scenes.tts: Its signal stops right now, because membrane now encloses the cytoplasmic tail completely. Cytosolic partners can no longer reach it, so signaling ends before digestion even begins. That step also places the whole receptor inside for breakdown.
scenes.caption: Its signal stops right now, because membrane now encloses the cytoplasmic tail completely. Cytosolic partners can no longer reach it, so signaling ends before digestion even begins. That step also places the whole receptor inside for breakdown.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. The glowing emerald halo on the enclosed receptor dims to muted grey (#94A3B8) with crisp label 'Tail sealed off'. Cytosolic partner blocks drift away from the outer membrane. A second and third internal vesicle bud inward, filling the multivesicular endosome.
scenes.narration: Its signal stops right now, because membrane now encloses the cytoplasmic tail completely. Cytosolic partners can no longer reach it, so signaling ends before digestion even begins. That step also places the whole receptor inside for breakdown.

scenes.tts: Meanwhile, cyan Rab five leaves as purple Rab seven arrives, a swap called Rab conversion. The late endosome grows more acid, then fuses with a lysosome near p H five. Each p H unit down means ten times more protons: seven to six is tenfold, seven to five a hundredfold.
scenes.caption: Meanwhile, cyan Rab5 leaves as purple Rab7 arrives, a swap called Rab conversion. The late endosome grows more acid, then fuses with a lysosome near pH 5. Each pH unit down means 10× more protons: 7 to 6 is 10×, 7 to 5 is 100×.
scenes.visual: On the same multivesicular endosome, cyan Rab5 tags (#38BDF8) detach while deep magenta-purple Rab7 tags (#E879F9, label 'Rab7 late endosome') populate the membrane. Beside it, a clean computed pH-to-proton scale builds in sync with narration: rule '1 pH unit down = 10× H⁺', then 'pH 7 → 1×', 'pH 6 → 10×' (amber), 'pH 5 → 100×' (deep coral-red), with a small tick 'late endosome ~5.5' (warm orange). Only after the lumen reaches orange does the late endosome fuse with a deep coral-red lysosome (label 'pH 4.5–5') filled with enzyme shapes that break down the internal vesicles.
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, cyan Rab5 leaves as purple Rab7 arrives, a swap called Rab conversion. The late endosome grows more acid, then fuses with a lysosome near pH 5. Each pH unit down means 10× more protons: 7 to 6 is 10×, 7 to 5 is 100×.

scenes.tts: Break that sorting tag, and signaling runs too long. In some lung cancers, the receptor M E T loses a short segment holding the docking site for its ubiquitin-adding enzyme. Left poorly tagged, M E T slips past Escort and keeps signaling.
scenes.caption: Break that sorting tag, and signaling runs too long. In some lung cancers, the receptor MET loses a short segment holding the docking site for its ubiquitin-adding enzyme. Left poorly tagged, MET slips past ESCRT and keeps signaling.
scenes.visual: Return to an early endosome showing an emerald receptor labelled 'MET (mutant)' with a small notched gap on its tail ('No ligase docking site', schematic). Gold ubiquitin beads (#FACC15) approach and only rarely attach; rose-red ESCRT clamps (#F43F5E) pass it by. The mutant MET stays on the outer endosome membrane, its emerald tail glowing brightly in the cytosol and continuing to send signal ripples.
scenes.narration: Break that sorting tag, and signaling runs too long. In some lung cancers, the receptor MET loses a short segment holding the docking site for its ubiquitin-adding enzyme. Left poorly tagged, MET slips past ESCRT and keeps signaling.

scenes.tts: Endocytosis alone does not turn an active receptor off. Mild acid can silence a receptor earlier if its ligand lets go. Otherwise, the way the tail faces sets the cutoff: active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.
scenes.caption: Endocytosis alone does not turn an active receptor off. Mild acid can silence a receptor earlier if its ligand lets go. Otherwise, the way the tail faces sets the cutoff: active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.
scenes.visual: Clean side-by-side summary inside the same endosome: on the outer membrane, an emerald receptor tail glows in the cytosol ('Active on outer wall'); inside an internal vesicle, a muted grey receptor sits enclosed ('Silenced inside vesicle'). Motion slows smoothly as the scene fades to dark slate.
scenes.narration: Endocytosis alone does not turn an active receptor off. Mild acid can silence a receptor earlier if its ligand lets go. Otherwise, the way the tail faces sets the cutoff: active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.

scenes.visual: Clean dark slate end card (#0F172A) with one centered line only (size 40, crisp white, no subtitle or secondary text): 'Active receptors can signal from endosomes until sealed inside internal vesicles.'
